idiom_name: internal sealed class with private readonly fields and file-scoped helpers
implementation_notes: C# hands over the boundary directly: top-level types default to `internal` (visible only inside the assembly), the `file` modifier restricts a type to its source file, `sealed` stops another contributor or assembly from re-attaching meaning through a subclass, and `private`/`private protected` keep state out of reach. A standalone class is therefore an ordinary `internal sealed class` with `private readonly` fields, a validating constructor and private or file-scoped helpers, so nothing of the surrounding model appears in its signature. Where the type is mainly data, the record form replaces the hand-written boilerplate; the classic class stays right when construction needs validation, the type has behaviour or identity, or the assembly must also be usable from older framework versions.
pitfalls: `internal` is only a boundary inside the assembly: any other type in the same assembly can use it, and `InternalsVisibleTo` widens it further, so in a large assembly the isolation still needs discipline.

The shape that serializers and ORMs want - a public parameterless constructor plus settable properties - makes every invariant optional; keep the validating constructor and configure mapping instead of weakening the type.
`private` members are invisible to reflection-based serialization by default, so persisting a fully encapsulated class needs explicit configuration or a DTO.
Mutable static state or an instance cache behind a public factory re-couples the type to the model's lifecycle and makes tests order-dependent.

variants.name: Positional record as the standalone value
variants.implementation_notes: Since C# 9 the language supplies the carrier: a positional `record` (or `readonly record struct`) declares the state and generates value equality, `ToString`, deconstruction and `with` copies, with `init`-only properties by default, so the type's semantics are exactly its declaration and no other model concept appears in it. Use it for standalone values (Money, Percentage, identifiers); add a body for validation, and choose `readonly record struct` for small values where copy semantics and stack allocation help. A sealed class remains the better shape when the type has behaviour beyond its data or must interop with mutable frameworks.
pitfalls: `with` copies are shallow: reference-typed members (arrays, collections) are shared with the copy, which breaks the value illusion unless the members are immutable.
A record can inherit only from another record and cannot derive from a normal class, so a record cannot be retrofitted onto an existing hierarchy.
A positional `record struct` is mutable by default - forgetting `readonly` leaves settable properties on a supposedly value-like type.
Serializers and ORMs that require a parameterless constructor or settable properties need explicit configuration for records.
